Dear brother, I have found my thoughts turning toward our father more often of late. It is true that we grieve differently. I was near a man when he passed, and had begun to see that I would soon be required to stand without him. You were still small enough that his absence came before that understanding. Even then, there are days when I remember the sound of his voice more clearly than the words themselves.

There are things a younger son must gather from watching rather than from being told. In these last weeks I have wondered whether I have done enough to stand where he once stood. 

It is a strange thing how a man begins to measure his own conduct against words he once scarcely understood. A man may follow an order and yet fail in his duty. Or suceed in his duty and fail an order.

I have received your letters. Several, at once. Not only because I was in the field these past weeks, but also because the post has grown irregular for reasons that will soon become clear to you. I have been in the barracks in Ufa these past days, recovering from the matter in the mountains. If this account lacks order, you must excuse it. I, however, am very glad to know you and great-aunt are well, and that your studies - despite everything - continue.
